high_level_description: A sealed source folio rests open for examination beside its identified press and one independent witness, yet remains outside the locked cabinet for corroborated bundles, in a wordless hand-colored woodcut inspired by Lyon’s Renaissance printer-gravers, with dense black cuts, muted vermilion, indigo and ochre, no text or arrows.

compositional_deconstruction.background: A single archive room adjoining a Renaissance printing workshop in Lyon, with pale limestone walls, exposed dark timber beams, one tall leaded-glass window and a worn gray flagstone floor. Cool-neutral daylight enters from the upper left and reaches every inspection surface. The room contains no wall sign, inscription, letter, numeral, caption, diagram, directional mark or heraldic emblem.

elements.desc: Tall Renaissance printing press standing at the upper left, built from dark oak with a screw platen, stone bed, frisket frame and folded drying cloth. A small brass rosette die is fixed beside the empty bed, matching the impression in the blue wax seal on the examined folio, while no second document remains inside the press.

Single source folio resting open in a low oak reading cradle, left of center. Cream pages show a black-ink river bridge with its central arch collapsed, without readable characters. An indigo cord and intact blue wax rosette remain attached from the origin press; the accessible binding stays physically outside the locked evidence cabinet.

Independent witness print standing separately beside the reading cradle, made from a copperplate and secured by a plain red circular seal. Its cream sheet shows the same river bridge and collapsed central arch from another viewpoint, but no second independent witness accompanies it. The different technique and seal keep its origin visibly distinct from the blue source.

Woman archivist kneeling between the two stands, medium-brown skin, dark braided hair covered by a cream linen cap, indigo gown, ochre apron and attentive neutral expression. She examines the blue-sealed source through a round brass lens while steadying the red-sealed witness with her other hand, making no approving gesture and touching neither cabinet nor key.

Locked iron-grille evidence cabinet standing at the right, separate from the open reading cradle, treated with its visible contents as one enclosure. Inside lies an older cream bundle bound by three cords and three different wax seals: red circle, blue rosette and ochre square. The newly read source remains outside; the shut door’s key hangs beyond the archivist’s reach.
